title: Driving the High-Level Design
summary: Turning clarified requirements into a first-pass architecture diagram, and iterating it live as the conversation reveals more.

slides.markdown:
Once [requirements are clarified](clarifying-requirements), the next job is turning them into boxes and arrows — a first-pass architecture that's deliberately rough, not a finished blueprint. The skill isn't drawing a perfect diagram on the first try; it's drawing a defensible starting point and reshaping it live as new constraints surface.

This topic covers how to go from requirements to a sketch, how to name what you're drawing, and how to keep revising it instead of treating it as done.

slides.sectionTitle: Going from requirements straight to a first-pass architecture
slides.markdown:
The fastest reliable path from requirements to a diagram is to draw one box per major responsibility your requirements named, then connect them in the order a request would actually flow. For a URL shortener: a client, an API layer, a service that generates and looks up short codes, and a datastore — four boxes, one arrow chain.

Resist the urge to add components you haven't justified yet, like a message queue or a cache, before you've shown why the simple version breaks. Adding "just in case" infrastructure early is a common tell that a candidate is pattern-matching to a template rather than deriving the design from the stated requirements.

The first pass should look almost too simple — that's what leaves room to justify every addition afterward.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a first-draft high-level diagram — boxes and arrows only
slides.markdown:
![Minimal first-draft URL shortener: Client, API layer, Shortening Service, Datastore](assets/minimal-first-draft.svg)

A good first draft has just enough boxes to satisfy the stated requirements, and nothing added on speculation. It looks almost too plain — which is exactly the point, since every box you add after this one should come with a stated reason.

Compare this to the [scale cube](scalability-fundamentals) idea: your first draft is the un-scaled version; everything you add next is a scaling decision you can defend.

slides.sectionTitle: Naming components by responsibility, not by product name
slides.markdown:
Label boxes by what they *do* — "rate limiter," "session store," "write-ahead queue" — rather than by a specific product like "Redis" or "Kafka" written into the diagram itself. Responsibility-first naming keeps the conversation about trade-offs, not brand loyalty, and makes it trivial to swap the implementation later without redrawing anything.

It also protects you from a common trap: naming a box "Redis" commits you to defending every property of that specific product, even ones you didn't mean to invoke. Naming it "cache" lets you say "an in-memory cache — Redis or Memcached would both work, I'd lean Redis for the built-in data structures" as a follow-up, which is a stronger answer than either name alone.

Say the product name once, as a detail on top of the responsibility — never as the label itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Iterating the diagram as new requirements surface
slides.markdown:
A high-level design is a living sketch for the whole interview, not a one-time deliverable — expect to redraw parts of it after estimation reveals a bottleneck, or after the interviewer asks a question your first pass didn't account for.

When a new requirement surfaces mid-conversation — "actually, this needs to work across two regions" — the right move is to point at the specific box that changes and explain the delta, not to erase and restart. "That affects the datastore box — I'd add cross-region replication here" keeps the existing work visible and shows you're updating a model, not guessing from scratch each time.

Candidates who treat the first diagram as final tend to defend it past the point it makes sense; candidates who treat it as a draft tend to score better on adaptability.

There are two defensible orders for building the diagram, and mixing them up mid-interview is what causes trouble.

| | Broad-then-narrow | Deep-then-broad |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Sketch the whole system first, then deep-dive one part | Fully design one path first, then extend to the rest |
| Risk if time runs out | Whole system is sketched, one area shallow | Some paths never get sketched at all |
| Best for | Most system design rounds — interviewer expects full coverage | A question explicitly scoped to one flow, e.g. "just design the write path" |
| Interviewer's default expectation | This one | Only if they said so |

**How to decide:** default to broad-then-narrow unless the interviewer explicitly scoped the question to one path — running out of time having covered nothing end-to-end is the worse failure mode of the two.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: drawing a polished diagram that never gets revisited or challenged
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If I get the diagram right the first time, I won't need to change it — that shows I planned well."

**Why it's wrong:** an interview diagram that never changes usually means the candidate stopped listening for new information, not that the first draft was perfect. Interviewers often introduce a constraint specifically to see whether you'll update the design or defend the original sketch out of attachment to it.

**Correct model:** treat every addition to the diagram as expected, not as a correction of a mistake. Redrawing a box after new information is a sign you're tracking the conversation, and it costs far less credibility than defending a design that's stopped fitting the requirements.

slides.sectionTitle: Sizing a component before you draw its box
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
Before a box goes on the board, it helps to know roughly how big that component needs to be — sizing the design before drawing it stops you from drawing something that quietly can't hold the load.

Concrete example: if requirements clarify 4,000 reads/sec and a 3TB dataset over five years, that already tells you the datastore box needs to be something that handles both — a single Postgres instance can serve 4,000 QPS of simple key lookups comfortably, but 3TB with growth suggests planning for read replicas or sharding within the diagram from the start, rather than drawing one database box and discovering later it doesn't fit.

The takeaway: let the numbers from the requirements phase decide how many boxes a tier needs, instead of drawing one box per tier by convention and fixing capacity later.

slides.sectionTitle: Staff-level nuance: when a monolith-first HLD is the stronger answer
slides.markdown:
Drawing five microservices for a system that could run as a well-organized monolith is a common way candidates think they're showing sophistication while actually showing weaker judgment. A staff-level answer states directly when a monolith-first HLD is the stronger call: at low team size and moderate scale, a modular monolith is faster to build, easier to debug (one process, one log stream, no network calls between your own components), and easier to change as requirements shift.

The signal to switch to services is organizational or scaling pressure, not aesthetics — multiple teams needing independent deploys, or one component's load profile genuinely diverging from the rest (e.g., a video-transcoding job that needs to scale independently of the API).

**Testing:** whether you default to the simplest architecture that meets the stated requirements, and can name specifically what would force you to split it up.
